1.summary: Paul thanks God for the Corinthians' gifts, then confronts their divisions around favorite leaders, and declares that the message of the cross, foolishness to the world, is God's power and wisdom, which is why God chose the weak and lowly.
1.lookfor: Notice the slogans the factions use, and how Paul turns the world's ideas of wisdom and strength upside down.

names.name: Sosthenes
names.gloss: Paul's co-sender, perhaps the synagogue leader beaten in Corinth.

names.name: Corinth
names.gloss: A wealthy, cosmopolitan port city in southern Greece.

names.name: Chloe
names.gloss: A woman whose household brought news of the quarrels.

names.name: Apollos
names.gloss: An eloquent teacher who had ministered in Corinth after Paul.

names.name: Cephas
names.gloss: Peter's Aramaic name.

names.name: Crispus
names.gloss: The former synagogue ruler Paul baptized.

names.name: Gaius
names.gloss: A believer Paul baptized, later his host.

names.name: Stephanas
names.gloss: Head of the first household to believe in Achaia.

insights.title: Corinth
insights.body: Corinth was a Roman colony rebuilt in 44 BC, a busy trading city full of new money, competing philosophers and status-seeking. Many of the church's problems mirror the city's values.

insights.title: Sanctified, called to be saints
insights.body: Paul addresses this troubled church as those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints (1:2), and thanks God for them (1:4). He starts with what God has done before what they've done wrong.

insights.title: Party slogans
insights.body: I follow Paul, I follow Apollos, I follow Cephas, I follow Christ (1:12). In Corinth, students were loyal to their favorite speakers like fans; the church copied that rivalry.

insights.title: Why Paul is glad he baptized few
insights.body: Paul thanks God he baptized only a few of them, so no one could say they were baptized in his name (1:14-15). Christ didn't send him mainly to baptize but to preach.

insights.title: The foolishness of the cross
insights.body: The word of the cross is foolishness to those perishing (1:18). Crucifixion was the most shameful death in the Roman world; polite people didn't mention it. A crucified Messiah sounded absurd.

insights.title: Not many wise
insights.body: Not many of you were wise, powerful or well-born (1:26). God chose the foolish, weak and despised so that no one can boast before him; whoever boasts should boast in the Lord.

insights.title: Following people
insights.body: The Corinthians attached themselves to favorite leaders. Is there a teacher or style you've made more central than Christ himself?

2.summary: Paul reminds them that he came not with impressive speech but resolved to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ crucified; true wisdom is God's hidden wisdom revealed by the Spirit to those who have the Spirit.
2.lookfor: Notice how Paul describes his own weakness when he first came, and the contrast between natural and spiritual people.

insights.title: Christ crucified
insights.body: Paul determined to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (2:2). In a city that prized eloquence, he deliberately chose plain words so their faith would rest on God's power.

insights.title: Weakness and trembling
insights.body: Paul came in weakness, fear and much trembling (2:3), probably after being driven out of Macedonian cities and getting a mixed response in Athens.

insights.title: No eye has seen
insights.body: Things no eye has seen and no ear has heard, God prepared for those who love him (2:9), echoing Isaiah. Often read of heaven, Paul applies it to what God has already revealed by his Spirit.

insights.title: Only the Spirit knows
insights.body: Just as only a person's spirit knows their thoughts, only God's Spirit knows God's thoughts (2:11). We understand God's gifts because he has given us his Spirit.

insights.title: Natural and spiritual
insights.body: The natural person, psychikos, doesn't receive the things of God's Spirit (2:14). The spiritual person is not an elite mystic but anyone led by the Spirit.

insights.title: The mind of Christ
insights.body: Who has known the Lord's mind? But we have Christ's mind (2:16), quoting Isaiah. Believers together are given a new way of thinking.

insights.title: Strength in weakness
insights.body: Paul's nervousness didn't stop God working. Where might your sense of inadequacy actually be room for God's power?

3.summary: Paul calls the Corinthians spiritual infants whose quarrels show they are still worldly; he and Apollos are only servants, God gives the growth; each worker's building on the one foundation will be tested by fire, and they themselves are God's temple.
3.lookfor: Notice the farming and building pictures, and the warning about the temple.

names.name: Apollos
names.gloss: A gifted teacher who watered what Paul planted.

names.name: Cephas
names.gloss: Peter.

insights.title: Milk, not solid food
insights.body: Paul fed them milk because they weren't ready for solid food, and still aren't (3:2). Their jealousy and strife prove they're acting merely human.

insights.title: God gives the growth
insights.body: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase (3:6). Leaders are only workers in God's field; rivalry between them makes no sense.

insights.title: The one foundation
insights.body: No one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, Jesus Christ (3:11). Jesus spoke of building on rock.

insights.title: Tested by fire
insights.body: Each one's work will be tested by fire: gold, silver and precious stones survive; wood, hay and straw burn (3:12-15). The builder is saved even if the work is lost, but as through fire.

insights.title: You are God's temple
insights.body: Don't you know you are God's temple, and God's Spirit lives in you? (3:16). The you is plural: the church together is the temple. Destroying it through division is serious.

insights.title: All things are yours
insights.body: Don't boast in people, for all things are yours: Paul, Apollos, Cephas, the world, life, death, and you are Christ's (3:21-23). Why pick one leader when God has given you all of them?

insights.title: What you're building
insights.body: Paul asks what kind of material people build with. What in your life will last, and what is straw?

4.summary: Paul says he and other apostles are servants and stewards who answer only to the Lord; with sharp irony he contrasts the Corinthians' self-satisfied pride with the apostles' hunger and dishonor, and as their father in Christ urges them to imitate him.
4.lookfor: Notice the irony in verses 8 to 13 and the father image at the end.

names.name: Timothy
names.gloss: Paul's beloved and faithful son in the Lord, being sent to Corinth.

insights.title: Stewards
insights.body: Regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries (4:1). A steward was a household manager, often a slave, entrusted with the owner's goods. The one thing required is faithfulness.

insights.title: I don't even judge myself
insights.body: Paul says it matters little to be judged by them, and he doesn't even judge himself; the Lord judges (4:3-4). He's free from both others' verdicts and his own.

insights.title: What do you have?
insights.body: What do you have that you didn't receive? And if you received it, why boast? (4:7). Every gift is a gift.

insights.title: A spectacle
insights.body: God has exhibited the apostles last of all, like men sentenced to death, a spectacle to the world (4:9). The picture is of a Roman triumph or the arena, where condemned prisoners came last.

insights.title: Already kings?
insights.body: Already you are full, already rich, already reigning without us! (4:8). Paul mocks a faith that thinks it has arrived, while apostles go hungry, homeless and cursed.

insights.title: Fathers and tutors
insights.body: You may have ten thousand tutors, but not many fathers; I became your father through the gospel (4:15). The tutor was a slave who supervised children; a father's care went deeper.

insights.title: Received, not achieved
insights.body: Paul asks what you have that you didn't receive. Which of your strengths do you tend to treat as your own achievement?

5.summary: Paul is shocked that the church tolerates a man living with his father's wife; he tells them to remove him so that he may ultimately be saved, compares sin to yeast that spreads, and clarifies that judgment is for those inside the church, not outsiders.
5.lookfor: Notice the Passover imagery and the difference between judging insiders and outsiders.

insights.title: Not even among pagans
insights.body: A man has his father's wife, likely his stepmother, a sin not even tolerated among Gentiles (5:1). Roman law also forbade it.

insights.title: Puffed up
insights.body: Worse than the sin is the church's pride about it (5:2). Perhaps they saw it as freedom in Christ.

insights.title: Hand him over
insights.body: Paul says to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord (5:5). The removal from the community aims at his repentance and final rescue, not his ruin.

insights.title: Christ our Passover
insights.body: A little yeast leavens the whole lump; clean out the old yeast, for Christ our Passover has been sacrificed (5:6-7). Before Passover, Jewish families swept every crumb of leaven from their houses.

insights.title: Sincerity and truth
insights.body: Keep the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (5:8). The word for sincerity suggests something held up to the sunlight and found pure.

insights.title: Inside and outside
insights.body: Paul didn't mean to avoid all immoral people in the world, or you'd have to leave the world (5:10). The church judges itself, not outsiders; God judges those outside.

insights.title: Small yeast
insights.body: Paul warns that a little yeast works through the whole batch. What small compromise could spread further than you expect?

6.summary: Paul rebukes believers for suing each other before pagan courts, reminds them that the unrighteous won't inherit God's kingdom but that they were washed and justified, and argues that their bodies belong to the Lord, so they must flee sexual immorality.
6.lookfor: Notice the Corinthian slogans Paul quotes and answers, and the high view of the body.

insights.title: Lawsuits
insights.body: Roman courts favored the wealthy, and lawsuits were a way to gain status. Paul is appalled that believers drag one another before unbelievers (6:1, 6:6). Better to be wronged.

insights.title: Such were some of you
insights.body: After a list of those who won't inherit the kingdom, Paul says, such were some of you, but you were washed, sanctified, justified (6:11). The list describes the past, not the present.

insights.title: All things are lawful
insights.body: All things are lawful for me (6:12) was likely a Corinthian slogan. Paul answers: but not all things are helpful, and I won't be mastered by anything.

insights.title: One flesh
insights.body: Joining yourself to a prostitute makes you one body with her, for the two shall become one flesh (6:16), from Genesis. Sex binds persons, not just bodies.

insights.title: Temple of the Spirit
insights.body: Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (6:19). In chapter 3 the church was the temple; here each body is. Corinth's temples were associated with immorality; this temple is holy.

insights.title: Bought with a price
insights.body: You aren't your own, for you were bought with a price; therefore glorify God in your body (6:19-20). Some Corinthians thought the body didn't matter; Paul says God redeemed it and will raise it.

insights.title: Your body matters
insights.body: Paul says your body belongs to God and is meant to honor him. How does that change how you treat your body this week?

7.summary: Answering their questions, Paul teaches that married couples should not deprive each other, that the unmarried and widowed may remain single or marry, that believers shouldn't initiate divorce, and that each should live the life the Lord assigned, while noting the advantages of singleness in a time of distress.
7.lookfor: Notice where Paul distinguishes his own advice from the Lord's command, and his balanced view of singleness and marriage.

insights.title: Now about the things you wrote
insights.body: Paul begins answering their letter (7:1). It is good for a man not to touch a woman was likely their slogan; some Corinthians thought sex itself was unspiritual, even within marriage.

insights.title: Mutual
insights.body: The wife doesn't have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise the husband doesn't have authority over his own body, but the wife (7:4). In a culture that gave husbands rights over wives, the mutuality was striking.

insights.title: Not I, but the Lord
insights.body: Paul carefully marks the difference between Jesus' command on divorce (7:10) and his own apostolic counsel (7:12, 7:25). He knows Jesus' teaching and builds on it.

insights.title: Sanctified by the believer
insights.body: A believer married to an unbeliever shouldn't leave, because the unbelieving spouse and the children are sanctified through the believer (7:14). Faith doesn't defile a mixed marriage; it can bless it.

insights.title: Gifts
insights.body: Paul wishes all were as he is, single, but each has their own gift from God, one this way, another that (7:7). Both marriage and singleness are gifts.

insights.title: The present distress
insights.body: Because of the present distress and because the time is short (7:26, 7:29), Paul advises people to stay as they are. This world in its present form is passing away (7:31).

insights.title: Undistracted
insights.body: Paul wants believers to serve the Lord without distraction (7:35). What distracts you most from wholehearted devotion?

8.summary: On food offered to idols, Paul agrees that idols are nothing and there is one God and one Lord, but warns that knowledge puffs up while love builds up; the strong must not use their freedom in a way that destroys a weaker believer.
8.lookfor: Notice the confession of one God and one Lord in verse 6, and Paul's personal resolve at the end.

insights.title: Food offered to idols
insights.body: Most meat sold in Corinth had passed through a temple sacrifice, and social life revolved around dinners in temple dining rooms. Refusing could cost friendships and business.

insights.title: Knowledge puffs up
insights.body: Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up (8:1). The Corinthians are right that idols are nothing, but being right isn't enough.

insights.title: One God, one Lord
insights.body: For us there is one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ (8:6). Paul rewrites Israel's central confession, the Shema, placing Jesus within the identity of the one God.

insights.title: The weak conscience
insights.body: Someone who used to worship idols might see you eating in a temple and be drawn back into idolatry (8:7, 8:10). Your freedom can become their stumbling block.

insights.title: Sinning against Christ
insights.body: When you wound a weak brother's conscience, you sin against Christ (8:12), for whom that brother died. The value of a person is measured by the cross.

insights.title: Stumbling block
insights.body: The word for stumbling block, proskomma, is something you trip over. Paul vows never to eat meat again if it makes his brother stumble (8:13).

insights.title: Right but unloving
insights.body: Paul says being right isn't the goal; building others up is. Where have you been right in a way that hurt someone?

9.summary: Paul defends his rights as an apostle to be supported, explains that he gave them up so as not to hinder the gospel, becoming all things to all people, and compares the Christian life to an athlete training for an imperishable crown.
9.lookfor: Notice why Paul refuses payment, and the athletic images at the end.

names.name: Barnabas
names.gloss: Paul's former partner, who also worked to support himself.

names.name: Cephas
names.gloss: Peter, who travelled with his wife.

names.name: Moses
names.gloss: The lawgiver, quoted about the ox.

insights.title: Why this chapter?
insights.body: Paul uses himself as an example for chapter 8: he has real rights as an apostle (9:4-6) but sets them aside for others' sake, just as the strong should set aside their right to eat.

insights.title: Don't muzzle the ox
insights.body: Paul quotes the law: you shall not muzzle the ox while it treads the grain (9:9). If even oxen may eat from their work, how much more those who labor in the gospel.

insights.title: Cephas's wife
insights.body: Paul mentions that the other apostles, the Lord's brothers and Cephas take believing wives along on their travels (9:5). A small window into Peter's family life.

insights.title: Necessity is laid on me
insights.body: Woe is me if I don't preach the gospel (9:16). Paul's reward is to preach without charge, so the gospel costs its hearers nothing.

insights.title: All things to all people
insights.body: To the Jews I became as a Jew, to those without the law as without the law, to the weak as weak: I have become all things to all people, that I might by all means save some (9:20-22). Flexible in method, fixed in message.

insights.title: The Isthmian Games
insights.body: Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, second only to the Olympics. Athletes trained strictly for a pine wreath that withered; believers run for an imperishable crown (9:24-25).

insights.title: Giving up rights
insights.body: Paul gave up what he was entitled to for the sake of others. What right could you give up so someone else might come closer to Christ?

10.summary: Paul warns from Israel's wilderness history that privileges don't prevent falling, so flee idolatry; one can't share the Lord's table and the table of demons; seek others' good, eat what is sold in the market, and do everything for God's glory.
10.lookfor: Notice the parallels between Israel's experience and the church's baptism and Supper, and the promise about temptation.

names.name: Moses
names.gloss: The leader under whom Israel passed through the sea.

names.name: Israel
names.gloss: God's people in the wilderness, an example to the church.

insights.title: Baptized into Moses
insights.body: Israel was baptized into Moses in the cloud and the sea, and ate spiritual food and drank from the spiritual rock, and the rock was Christ (10:1-4). Yet most of them died in the wilderness.

insights.title: Written for us
insights.body: These things happened as examples and were written for our instruction (10:6, 10:11). The Corinthians felt secure because of their sacraments; Israel had the same privileges and still fell.

insights.title: A way of escape
insights.body: No temptation has taken you except what is common to people; God is faithful and will provide a way of escape (10:13). The way out often comes with the temptation, not after it.

insights.title: Participation
insights.body: The cup of blessing is a sharing, koinonia, in Christ's blood, and the bread a sharing in his body (10:16). Because we share one bread, we who are many are one body (10:17).

insights.title: The table of demons
insights.body: Pagan sacrifices are offered to demons; you can't drink the Lord's cup and the cup of demons (10:20-21). Temple dinners were religious events, not neutral meals.

insights.title: For God's glory
insights.body: Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God (10:31). Even ordinary meals become worship.

insights.title: Thinking you stand
insights.body: Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall (10:12). Where might you be overconfident about your own strength?

11.summary: Paul addresses head coverings in worship, grounding his instructions in creation and custom, then rebukes the Corinthians for turning the Lord's Supper into a meal where the rich eat first and the poor go hungry, retelling Jesus' words at the Last Supper.
11.lookfor: Notice why Paul says their meetings do more harm than good, and the earliest written account of the Lord's Supper.

insights.title: Head coverings
insights.body: In the Roman world, a married woman's head covering signaled modesty and marital status; uncovered hair could send other messages. Paul wants worship that doesn't scandalize (11:5-6).

insights.title: Praying and prophesying
insights.body: Paul assumes women pray and prophesy in worship (11:5); his concern is how, not whether. Readers still debate how these instructions apply today.

insights.title: Interdependent
insights.body: Neither is woman independent of man, nor man of woman, in the Lord; as woman came from man, so man comes through woman, and all things are from God (11:11-12).

insights.title: The house-church meal
insights.body: Wealthy hosts served their peers in the dining room while others crowded the courtyard, and the poor, who arrived late after work, found food gone (11:21). Roman dinner parties ranked guests by status.

insights.title: Do this in remembrance
insights.body: Paul passes on what he received: on the night he was betrayed, Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it (11:23-25). Written before the Gospels, this is the oldest record of the Lord's Supper.

insights.title: Discerning the body
insights.body: Whoever eats without discerning the body eats judgment on himself (11:29). In context, the body likely includes the church: despising the poor at the table ignores Christ's body.

insights.title: Waiting for one another
insights.body: Paul's practical fix: when you come together to eat, wait for one another (11:33). Who might be left out at your table?

12.summary: Paul explains that there are many gifts but one Spirit, given to each for the common good, and that the church is one body with many members, each necessary, the weaker ones indispensable, all suffering and rejoicing together.
12.lookfor: Notice the variety of gifts, and the humorous picture of body parts talking to each other.

names.name: Jews
names.gloss: Members of Israel, baptized with Gentiles into one body.

names.name: Greeks
names.gloss: Gentiles.

insights.title: Jesus is Lord
insights.body: No one can say Jesus is Lord except by the Holy Spirit (12:3). The basic Christian confession is itself a work of the Spirit, so every believer has him.

insights.title: Gifts
insights.body: The word for gifts, charismata, comes from charis, grace (12:4). Gifts are grace given, not achievements to display.

insights.title: For the common good
insights.body: To each is given the Spirit's manifestation for the profit of all (12:7). The Corinthians valued gifts that impressed; Paul values gifts that serve.

insights.title: The body politic
insights.body: Roman speakers used the body image to keep lower classes in their place: the stomach needs the hands. Paul flips it: the parts that seem weaker are indispensable, and God gives greater honor to the lesser (12:22-24).

insights.title: If the foot said
insights.body: If the foot says, because I'm not a hand I'm not part of the body, it's still part of the body (12:15). If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? (12:17).

insights.title: One body
insights.body: We were all baptized by one Spirit into one body, Jews or Greeks, slaves or free (12:13). When one member suffers, all suffer; when one is honored, all rejoice (12:26).

insights.title: Your part
insights.body: Paul says no part of the body can say it doesn't need the others. Which members of your church do you overlook, and what gift do you hold back?

13.summary: Paul describes the more excellent way: without love, the greatest gifts and sacrifices are nothing; love is patient and kind, never fails; gifts will pass away, but faith, hope and love remain, and the greatest is love.
13.lookfor: Notice how the description of love reads like a portrait, and the contrast between what passes and what remains.

insights.title: Why here?
insights.body: This isn't a wedding poem dropped in; it's at the center of Paul's argument about gifts (chapters 12 to 14). The Corinthians had gifts but lacked love.

insights.title: A clanging cymbal
insights.body: Without love, tongues are a resounding gong or a clanging cymbal (13:1). Bronze instruments were used noisily in pagan worship; Corinth was known for bronze work.

insights.title: Agapē
insights.body: The word for love, agapē, was rare in Greek before the New Testament. Christians filled it with meaning from the cross: self-giving love that seeks the other's good.

insights.title: A portrait
insights.body: Love is patient, kind, not envious, not boastful, not proud (13:4-7). Each phrase answers a Corinthian problem. Many readers find that putting Jesus' name in place of love fits perfectly.

insights.title: In a mirror dimly
insights.body: Now we see in a mirror, dimly (13:12). Ancient mirrors were polished bronze and gave a blurred image, ironically another Corinthian product. Then we'll see face to face.

insights.title: Faith, hope, love
insights.body: Faith, hope and love remain, and the greatest of these is love (13:13). Gifts are for this age; love belongs to the age to come.

insights.title: Where love fails
insights.body: Read verses 4 to 7 slowly. Which quality of love is hardest for you right now, and toward whom?

14.summary: Paul urges them to pursue prophecy over uninterpreted tongues because it builds up the church, insists that worship be intelligible to outsiders, and gives guidelines for orderly meetings where everyone contributes, since God is not a God of confusion.
14.lookfor: Notice how often Paul uses the words build up and edify, and his concern for outsiders.

insights.title: Edify
insights.body: The key word is build up, oikodomē, house-building (14:3-5, 14:12, 14:26). Every gift in worship is measured by whether it builds others up.

insights.title: Five words with understanding
insights.body: In church Paul would rather speak five words with understanding than ten thousand in a tongue (14:19), though he speaks in tongues more than all of them (14:18).

insights.title: Ecstatic religion
insights.body: Corinth knew pagan cults where frenzy and ecstatic speech proved divine possession. Paul says the spirits of prophets are subject to the prophets (14:32): the Spirit doesn't override self-control.

insights.title: Think of the outsider
insights.body: If an unbeliever walks in and everyone speaks in tongues, they'll say you're mad; if all prophesy, they'll be convicted and fall down saying God is truly among you (14:23-25).

insights.title: Other tongues
insights.body: Paul quotes Isaiah: by people of strange tongues I will speak to this people, and they still won't listen (14:21). Unintelligible speech was a sign of judgment, not of welcome.

insights.title: Decently and in order
insights.body: God is not a God of confusion but of peace (14:33); let all things be done decently and in order (14:40). Each person brings something (14:26), but everything serves building up.

insights.title: Building up
insights.body: Paul measured every contribution by whether it helped others. When you gather with believers, what do you bring that builds someone up?

15.summary: Paul restates the gospel he received, lists the witnesses of the risen Christ, argues that if Christ isn't raised faith is futile, explains the order of the resurrection and the nature of the resurrection body, and ends in triumph over death.
15.lookfor: Notice the early creed in verses 3 to 5, the long list of witnesses, and the seed image for the resurrection body.

names.name: Cephas
names.gloss: Peter, the first named witness of the risen Jesus.

names.name: James
names.gloss: The Lord's brother, who saw the risen Jesus.

names.name: Adam
names.gloss: The first man, contrasted with Christ, the last Adam.

insights.title: An early creed
insights.body: Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Cephas (15:3-5). Paul received this formula, probably within a few years of the resurrection.

insights.title: Five hundred at once
insights.body: Jesus appeared to over five hundred at once, most of whom are still alive (15:6). Paul is in effect saying: go ask them.

insights.title: If Christ isn't raised
insights.body: If Christ hasn't been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins (15:17). Some Corinthians, influenced by Greek ideas, denied a bodily resurrection; Paul says everything stands or falls on it.

insights.title: Firstfruits
insights.body: Christ is the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (15:20). The first sheaf of harvest was offered to God as a promise of the full harvest to come.

insights.title: The last Adam
insights.body: The first man Adam became a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit (15:45). As we bore the image of the man of dust, we will bear the image of the heavenly man.

insights.title: Death, where is your sting?
insights.body: Death is swallowed up in victory. Death, where is your sting? (15:54-55), from Isaiah and Hosea. So be steadfast; your labor in the Lord is not in vain (15:58).

insights.title: Not in vain
insights.body: Because of the resurrection, Paul says your work for the Lord is never wasted. What work have you been tempted to think was pointless?

16.summary: Paul gives instructions for the collection for Jerusalem, shares his travel plans, commends Timothy, Apollos and the household of Stephanas, and closes with greetings, a curse on those who don't love the Lord, and the Aramaic prayer for the Lord to come.
16.lookfor: Notice the practical plan for giving and the short charge in verses 13 and 14.

names.name: Galatia
names.gloss: A Roman province in central Asia Minor.

names.name: Ephesus
names.gloss: Where Paul was writing from.

names.name: Stephanas
names.gloss: Leader of the first household of believers in Achaia.

names.name: Fortunatus
names.gloss: A Corinthian believer who visited Paul.

names.name: Achaicus
names.gloss: A Corinthian believer who visited Paul.

names.name: Aquila
names.gloss: Priscilla's husband; their house church met in Ephesus.

insights.title: The first day of the week
insights.body: On the first day of every week, each should set aside something as they have prospered (16:2). Regular, proportional giving, tied to the day of the resurrection.

insights.title: A wide door
insights.body: Paul will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, for a great and effective door has opened to him, and there are many adversaries (16:8-9). Opportunity and opposition come together.

insights.title: Apollos declined
insights.body: Paul strongly urged Apollos to visit, but he was unwilling now (16:12). No rivalry between the two men, whatever the Corinthian factions said.

insights.title: Let all be done in love
insights.body: Watch, stand firm in the faith, be courageous, be strong; let all that you do be done in love (16:13-14). The whole letter in a sentence.

insights.title: Maranatha
insights.body: Paul writes an Aramaic phrase, Marana tha, Our Lord, come (16:22). That Greek-speaking Corinthians knew it shows the earliest believers were already praying to Jesus as Lord in Aramaic.

insights.title: My love to all
insights.body: After a letter of rebukes, Paul's last words are my love be with all of you in Christ Jesus (16:24). Correction came from love.

insights.title: Regular giving
insights.body: Paul asked for planned, regular giving. What would generous, planned giving look like for you?

intro.who: Paul wrote it, with Sosthenes (1:1), to the church he had founded in Corinth about five years earlier.
intro.when: About AD 53–55, from Ephesus (16:8), during Paul's third journey.
intro.why: The young church was divided into factions, tolerating serious sin, suing one another, confused about marriage, food offered to idols, worship, spiritual gifts and the resurrection. Paul answers reports and their letter of questions, calling them back to the cross and to love.
